# Results: household vulnerability clusters (BIHS Round 3)

*Draft results-section source generated by `visualize_clusters.py` on 2026-09-19. Figures in `figures/` (300 dpi). N = 5,605 households; K-Means, k = 2, on 9 retained PCs (81.2% of variance).*

## Cluster profiles

**Cluster 1 — “off-farm, single-livelihood, flood-spared (average-LVI)”.** This cluster contains 3,118 households (55.6% of the sample), with a mean LVI of 0.455 (95% CI ±0.002; median 0.450, SD 0.064, IQR 0.092), below the sample mean of 0.464 (Fig. 3). Its dimension scores are exposure 0.382, sensitivity 0.284 and adaptive-capacity vulnerability 0.700 (sample: 0.452, 0.301, 0.638). Its defining traits (|SMD| ≥ 0.30 on the normalized indicators; Fig. 2) are: agri-occupation dependence 0.11 vs sample 0.45 (SMD -0.56, less vulnerable); livelihood diversity 0.39 vs sample 0.72 (SMD +0.53, more vulnerable); flood affected (0/1) 0.31 vs sample 0.57 (SMD -0.52, less vulnerable); cultivable land (dec) 20.66 vs sample 65.74 (SMD +0.48, more vulnerable); flood depth (ft) 0.58 vs sample 1.31 (SMD -0.39, less vulnerable); non-farm work (0/1) 0.08 vs sample 0.22 (SMD +0.33, more vulnerable). By LVI tertile, 40.4% of its households are Low, 32.1% Medium and 27.5% High (Fig. 6). Policy relevance: because this group's vulnerability stems from a thin asset and livelihood base rather than from hazard exposure, it is better served by asset-building, skills and off-farm income-diversification programmes than by flood-protection investment.

**Cluster 2 — “agriculture-dependent, diversified-livelihood, flood-exposed (average-LVI)”.** This cluster contains 2,487 households (44.4% of the sample), with a mean LVI of 0.474 (95% CI ±0.003; median 0.479, SD 0.064, IQR 0.083), above the sample mean of 0.464 (Fig. 3). Its dimension scores are exposure 0.540, sensitivity 0.322 and adaptive-capacity vulnerability 0.561 (sample: 0.452, 0.301, 0.638). Its defining traits (|SMD| ≥ 0.30 on the normalized indicators; Fig. 2) are: agri-occupation dependence 0.87 vs sample 0.45 (SMD +0.70, more vulnerable); livelihood diversity 1.14 vs sample 0.72 (SMD -0.66, less vulnerable); flood affected (0/1) 0.89 vs sample 0.57 (SMD +0.65, more vulnerable); cultivable land (dec) 122.27 vs sample 65.74 (SMD -0.61, less vulnerable); flood depth (ft) 2.23 vs sample 1.31 (SMD +0.49, more vulnerable); non-farm work (0/1) 0.39 vs sample 0.22 (SMD -0.41, less vulnerable). By LVI tertile, 24.5% of its households are Low, 34.9% Medium and 40.6% High (Fig. 6). Policy relevance: this group is the natural target for flood-risk reduction, crop insurance and climate-resilient agriculture, because its higher LVI is driven by exposure and sensitivity while its adaptive capacity is comparatively strong.

## Cluster-based versus index-based classification

The two vulnerability measures overlap only partially. Cluster membership and LVI tertile class are statistically associated (χ²(2) = 178.0, p = 2.3e-39), but the association is weak: Cramér's V = 0.18 and the Spearman correlation between cluster LVI-rank and tertile class is ρ = 0.18. The lower-LVI cluster (C1) holds 40.4% Low, 32.1% Medium and 27.5% High households, whereas the higher-LVI cluster (C2) holds 24.5%, 34.9% and 40.6% respectively (a uniform 33.3% would indicate no relationship). Put differently, 54.0% of all High-LVI households fall in C2 and 67.4% of all Low-LVI households fall in C1. The gap in mean LVI between clusters (0.019) is small relative to the within-cluster spread (SD 0.064 and 0.064; Fig. 5), and the boxplots show the two LVI distributions overlapping across almost their entire range. This divergence is informative rather than a failure of either measure. The LVI aggregates exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity additively, so a household that is highly flood-exposed but asset-rich can receive the same score as one that is flood-spared but land-poor and single-livelihood. The clustering separates precisely these two *types* of vulnerability: C2 is a hazard-exposed, agriculture-dependent group whose vulnerability is driven by exposure and sensitivity, while C1 is a flood-spared but capacity-constrained group whose vulnerability is driven by low adaptive capacity. The ordering of the clusters by mean LVI agrees with the index, which validates the direction of the LVI, but the composition of vulnerability, and therefore the appropriate policy response, differs between the two groups in a way that a single composite score cannot reveal. We therefore recommend reporting both: the LVI for ranking and targeting intensity, and the cluster typology for choosing the type of intervention.

## Methodological notes

- LVI tertile classes were not produced in Stage 1; they are defined here as sample terciles of the LVI (Low ≤ 0.4326 < Medium ≤ 0.4937 < High), giving n = 1,869 / 1,868 / 1,868.
- Radar axes (Fig. 2) use the Stage 1 min-max normalized indicators (0–1, oriented so higher = more vulnerable), so raw units (Tk, decimals, counts, 0/1) are directly comparable; the dashed line is the sample mean.
- Error bars in Fig. 3 are 95% t-based confidence intervals of the cluster mean; because n is large the CIs are narrow, so the boxplots in Fig. 5 should be used to judge the *practical* separation of the clusters.
- Cluster labels are numbered in ascending order of mean LVI (Stage 2 convention). Cluster names come from the Stage 2 report.
- Silhouette at k = 2 is 0.152 and the Ward robustness check gives ARI = 0.28 (Stage 2 report), so the clusters should be described as a two-type continuum rather than as sharply separated groups; Fig. 1 shows the overlap in PC space.
